newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar-China OKs up to 500,000T toll permits.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar-China OKs up to 500,000T toll permits.

text.p: China has issued up to 500,000 tonnes of sugar tolling licences and at least one cargo of sugar was currently loading, destined for a south China port, sugar traders in the region said on Wednesday.
"China has issued between 400,000 and 500,000 tonnes of tolling licences," a Hong Kong sugar trader said.
Japan-based traders concurred, but noted they had not heard that China was in the market and said they did not expect the news to move Thai premiums.
In Hong Kong, at least one cargo of 26,000 tonnes of sugar was heard currently loading in Australia, destined for south China where many of the country's large sugar mills are clustered.
The other 26,000 tonne cargo of Australian sugar earlier waiting at a south China port was now discharging, sugar sources in China said.

China had already covered its tolling requirement via Hong Kong traders, one dealer at a major Japanese trading firm said. "If China buys more sugar for tolling, the maxmium amounts would be around three cargos (36,000 tonnes) for the near term," the Tokyo-based trader said.

China awarded the sugar tolling licences over the last week to several companies, including trading firms and sugar refineries. Most of the volume went to China's main sugar import and export body, sources in Hong Kong and China said.
Tolling was still not profitable with the current levels of white and raws, dealers said, noting that the tolling licence awardees would simply sit and wait for prices to favour tolling.
"This will not have much of an impact on the market," one sugar trader said.
On an FOB China basis, Thai sugar was currently about $15 over London, and Chinese tolled sugar would be about $30-$40 over London, sugar traders estimated.
The domestic Chinese price of white sugar in Guangxi was still around 3,800 yuan ($458) per tonne, sources said.
In tolling, raw material is imported duty free if the final product is for re-export.
Asian sugar markets remained quiet amid a lack of significant physical offtake and sentiment remained bearish, Tokyo traders said.

Thai raw sugar premiums for April/May deliveries were quoted easier at 0.20/0.35 U.S. cents per pound (bid/offer) over New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) May futures on a FOB basis, compared with 0.40/0.50 U.S. cents a week ago.
May/July deliveries were quoted at 0.25/0.35 U.S. cents, against 0.40/0.50 U.S. cents a week ago. July/September deliveries were quoted at 0.50/0.60 cents, down from 0.60/0.70 U.S. cents a week ago.
One trader in Japan said Thai mills had refrained from selling sugar, anticipating firmer premiums.
"They will be forced to sell sugar soon when the sugar terminals have no space left for storage," he said.
